Article Title: SC rejects 1993 blast accused Abu Salem's plea for early release from life term
Article Text:
Salem was extradited from Portugal on November 11, 2005, after a prolonged legal battle.

The Supreme Court dismissed a plea by gangster Abu Salem on Thursday after he sought an early release from custody for having completed 25 years in jail.Salem, who is serving a sentence in connection with the 1993 Mumbai serial blasts, was extradited from Portugal on November 11, 2005, following a prolonged legal battle.The extradition agreement between India and Portugal stipulated that Salem could not be sentenced to death and that his prison term could not exceed 25 years.A bench comprising Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta upheld Bombay High Court’s April ruling, which had rejected his plea for immediate release, terming it “premature” and “misconceived”.A detailed order is yet to be released.Earlier in Feb, the Supreme Court refused to entertain Salem’s plea, which claimed that he was in "illegal custody" for over 10 months as he had already undergone the 25-year sentence awarded to him in the March 12, 1993, Mumbai serial bomb blasts case.
Article Summary: Abu salem is serving a sentence in connection with the 1993 mumbai serial blasts. He was extradited from portugal on november 11, 2005, following a prolonged legal battle. The extradition agreement between india and portugal stipulated that salem could not be sentenced to death and that his prison term could not exceed 25 years.

Article Title: West Asia conflict likely hindrance to cementing Brics declaration
Article Text:
West Asia conflict likely hindrance to cementing BRICS declaration

Cannot predict outcome of declaration: Russian minister

NEW DELHI: India’s push for agreement at the BRICS summit beginning Sept 12 faces divisions among its members over the West Asia conflict.Russian officials, speaking to their country’s media, have acknowledged difficult negotiations, while Brazilian reporting has raised doubts about a strong final declaration. Yet Chinese commentary has highlighted opportunities for India’s presidency, including closer trade ties. These contrasting accounts suggest that the challenge for New Delhi is to keep economic cooperation moving while finding language that countries with conflicting security interests can accept.The Sept 12–13 summit at Bharat Mandapam will bring these differences into focus. A final declaration records the common positions that participating countries have agreed to support.Russian deputy foreign minister Sergey Ryabkov told TASS that some members were sharply critical of Tehran’s actions, making the Gulf situation Brics’ most pressing political issue. “And as of today, I cannot predict what the outcome will be,” he said about negotiations on the final document.Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov acknowledged that Iran–UAE differences complicated drafting, but expressed confidence that diplomats would find acceptable wording.The disagreement concerns what members want Brics to say about the conflict. Iran’s Mehr agency reported its judiciary chief’s call at a preparatory meeting for condemnation of US–Israeli attacks. UAE agency WAM highlighted Emirati criticism of Iranian attacks on commercial shipping and demands to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.Chinese commentary has focused on India’s economic strengths. A Global Times article carried by People’s Daily praised its strengths in digital techn and medicine, while saying that bridging differences among members would test Indian diplomacy.Another Global Times commentary advocated deeper India–China trade and greater Chinese market access for Indian products. Indian reporting has highlighted New Delhi’s concerns about Chinese restrictions on critical technologies and industrial components.In Brazil, CNN Brasil reported that President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva would prioritise poll campaigning and send foreign minister Mauro Vieira. South Africa’s Business Day questioned whether expansion had weakened Brics’ unity, while broadcaster SABC highlighted Pretoria’s push for trade, industrialisation and African infra investment.For India, success would mean reaching useful agreements on specific issues while negotiating a common political message among partners whose interests do not always coincide.
Article Summary: West asia conflict likely hindrance to cementing brics declaration. Russian officials have acknowledged difficult negotiations. Brazilian reporting has raised doubts about a strong final declaration. Yet chinese commentary has highlighted opportunities for india’s presidency, including closer trade ties.

Article Title: Indians trust the classroom, see better opportunities abroad: Global survey
Article Text:

On use of AI

Not because the Ipsos Education Monitor survey mirrors the plot of the Shah Rukh Khan-Juhi Chawla film, but because the title neatly captures the contradiction in its India findings. Indians may believe better opportunities for growth and prosperity lie offshore, yet they remain remarkably bullish about their education system, their degrees and, above all, the future of their youth.More than half of Indian respondents rate the country’s education system as good. Three-fourths believe youth will have a better life than their parents. Nearly two-thirds think even young people from lesser privileged backgrounds have a bright future. And Indians remain strikingly convinced that a university degree still has value. However, ironically, 76% of Indian respondents say young people would have better opportunities by moving abroad.For some parameters, TOI looked at the subset of India’s position among the 16 individual G20 member countries included in the 31-country Ipsos survey. China, Russia and Saudi Arabia were not surveyed. The survey covered 23,537 online adults across the 31 countries between June and July 2026, with about 1,000 respondents in India.Ipsos in its methodology has cautioned that its India sample is more urban, educated and/or affluent than the general population and should be interpreted as reflecting the views of the country’s more “connected” segment.The 31-country average is an unweighted average of country results; it is not adjusted for the population size of each country.The first question was straightforward. How do people rate the overall quality of their country’s education system? In India, 51% called it good. Among the G20 countries covered by the survey, only Australia was higher, at 53%. The 31-country average was 33%. But that 51% is a number in retreat. India was at 65% in 2025, 69% in 2024 and 55% in 2023. The 14-point fall from 2025 is the steepest year-on-year decline among countries with comparable 2025 data.The contrast with several richer economies is sharp. Britain was at 43%, the US and Brazil at 32%, Italy at 29%, Japan at 24%, while France and Germany were both at 17%. That does not mean India has a better-performing education system than advanced economies. This is a matter of perception. And on that measure, Indians appear unusually confident. Just less than before.The gap becomes even more striking when the question shifts from institutions to the people coming out of them. Asked whether young people in their country have a bright future, 72% of Indian respondents agreed. That was not merely the highest figure among the G20 countries covered. It was the highest among all 31 countries surveyed. The 31-country average was 45%.Within the surveyed G20 set, Australia and South Africa were next at 54%, followed by Mexico at 52% and Canada at 50%. France was at 22%. It is perhaps one of the strongest votes of confidence in the survey. Indians appear to have placed enormous hope in their youth to put the country on the right track and take it forward.One of the hallmarks of an aspirational society like India is the belief in accumulating wealth and opportunity across generations. People believe that the hard work of one generation will make the lives of those that follow smoother. That belief gets backed in this survey. Three-fourths of Indian respondents, 75%, believe young people today will have a better life than their parents. The 31-country average is 48%.Indians are also optimistic about people escaping the poverty trap. 64% believe young people from poorer backgrounds have a bright future, compared with a 31-country average of 40%. India is the highest among the G20 countries covered on both measures. And 69% of Indian respondents believe the education system contributes to reducing social inequalities, again the highest among the surveyed G20 countries. That figure is also below earlier readings, 72% in 2024 and 79% in 2023.Together, these numbers suggest that Indian respondents continue to see education as a vehicle for upward social mobility. That belief becomes even clearer when the survey turns to higher education. NITI Aayog ’s recent report also points to the continuing pull of degree programmes, noting that vocational pathways are often not seen as credible, growth-oriented alternatives and that degrees can become the safer choice amid limited counselling, social bias and low trust in existing skill systems. The Ipsos survey, albeit with a more urban and connected Indian sample, points in a similar direction. 75% of Indian respondents say a college or university degree is very important to succeed in life. 78% believe it helps people go further in their careers. And 70% say degrees in their country offer good value for money.On the first measure, India is the highest among the G20 countries surveyed. On both the other measures, it ranks second. The contrast with several advanced economies is large. On whether a degree is good value for money, India’s 70% compares with 38% in the US, 41% in Germany, 30% in Japan and 28% in Britain. Ipsos itself finds a strong positive relationship across countries between believing that a degree helps a career and believing that it offers value for money.Here again, the Ipsos study broadly aligns with a concern flagged in NITI Aayog’s skilling report that education and credentials do not automatically translate into the skills and pathways that the labour market demands. The Ipsos survey shows a deep-seated faith in formal education and yet a growing realisation that job-market demands are at times different from what is being taught in the classroom.Asked whether the school curriculum adequately prepares students for future careers, 67% of Indians agree, the highest share among the G20 countries covered by the survey. Even here, the direction has been downward: 74% agreed in 2024, 72% in 2025 and 67% now.Yet in another question on the greatest challenges facing young people, 36% of Indian respondents select “education and training systems not matching labour market demands”. That too is the highest among the G20 countries in the survey.India again falls on one extreme of a scatter plot for its two seemingly contradictory sets of beliefs. On one hand, 72% say young people have a bright future. On the other hand, 76% say young people would have better opportunities by moving abroad. The 31-country average on that question is 62%.Indonesia and South Africa are even more likely to say opportunities are better overseas, at 87% and 80% respectively. Italy is at 79%. Romania matches India at 76%. But none combines that level of outward-looking aspiration with India’s exceptional optimism about the future of its young.This is perhaps the central finding of the entire report for India. Respondents may be optimistic about India’s young people precisely because they believe those young people possess education and skills that give them more options, including the option of leaving. The optimism may be about the people. The doubt may be about the location of opportunity.The dichotomy in the approach of Indians extends to technology too. 78% support banning social media for children under 14, both inside and outside school. The 31-country average is 73%.Support has climbed 10 points in a year. India was at 68% in 2025 and 73% in 2024.On smartphones, 57% of Indian respondents favour a ban in schools, exactly matching the 31-country average. That is up from 50% last year and 52% in 2024. But attitudes to AI are different.Only 26% of Indian respondents say AI, including ChatGPT, should be banned in schools, compared with 39% across the 31 countries. Indian opinion on AI has moved sharply over the four editions of the survey. 39% wanted AI banned in schools in both 2025 and 2024, compared with just 16% in 2023. The 13-point drop from 2025 to 2026 is the largest year-on-year fall among countries with comparable 2025 data.Britain, the US and Poland moved in the other direction, rising to 52%, 56% and 46%, respectively.To sum up, India’s ‘connected’ population has not lost faith in education. Quite the opposite. It remains unusually convinced that education matters, degrees pay, children can surpass their parents and those from poorer homes can climb. What appears less certain is where that promise will ultimately be realised.andmay finally be different. That is the sobering realisation one can derive from this survey.
Article Summary: More than half of indian respondents rate the country’s education system as good. Three-fourths believe youth will have a better life than their parents. Nearly two-thirds think even young people from lesser privileged backgrounds have a bright future. Three-fourths of indian respondents, 75%, believe young people today will have a better life than their parents.

NEW DELHI: Tamil Nadu chief minister and TVK chief C Joseph Vijay on Wednesday named his alliance with the Congress, VCK, MDMK and IUML the “Secular Social Justice Victory Alliance” as leaders of the parties met for the second time at the TVK headquarters in Chennai.TVK sources cited by news agency PTI had earlier confirmed that key alliance partners, including the Congress, Viduthalai Chiruthaigal Katchi (VCK), Indian Union Muslim League (IUML), and Marumalarchi Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (MDMK), would participate in the meeting.However, the CPM and CPI have decided to skip the meeting, marking their second consecutive boycott of formal alliance talks since July 1.Explaining the decision, CPM state secretary P Shanmugam said on Tuesday that the Left parties’ outside support would remain strictly issue-based, with the aim of maintaining stability in the Assembly.Adding to the tensions is a growing public rift between the TVK and the Congress over the question of national leadership.Statements from TVK legislators and ministers projecting chief minister Vijay as a potential Prime Ministerial candidate for the 2029 general elections have drawn strong opposition from Tamil Nadu Congress Committee (TNCC) leaders.Congress minister S Rajesh Kumar has firmly asserted that Rahul Gandhi remains the undisputed leader of the national opposition bloc. He warned that any attempt to undermine this consensus could prompt the party to reconsider its participation in the state cabinet.The TVK leadership subsequently sought to play down the controversy, maintaining that the “Vijay for PM” remarks reflected the personal views of individual lawmakers.

Article Title: Brics summit in Delhi on September 12-13: Agenda, schedule and other details
Article Text:

The two-day BRICS summit in New Delhi, set to kick-off Saturday, will focus on strengthening cooperation in food and energy security, health, disaster resilience and critical supply chains, as member countries seek to build greater resilience amid a fragmented geopolitical environment.The summit, hosted by India under its 2026 chairship, will also cover trade, investment, connectivity and technology, while leaders are expected to exchange views on major global and regional developments.Under India's resilience pillar, leaders will discuss cooperation in areas including health, agriculture, food and energy security, disaster-risk reduction and critical supply chains. The discussions come against the backdrop of disruptions caused by geopolitical conflicts and growing concerns over the resilience of global supply networks.Strengthening intra-BRICS trade and investment, improving connectivity and expanding cooperation in high technology will also be among the key economic priorities. India has placed these areas at the centre of its broader effort to deepen cooperation among emerging economies.The summit will also focus on strengthening multilateralism and making global governance more inclusive. The first closed-door session on Saturday is titled “Inclusive Global Governance and Strengthening Multilateralism.”Leaders will exchange views on global and regional developments and discuss areas of mutual interest, according to the Ministry of External Affairs.The main open session on Sunday is titled “Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability: Shaping the Future for Inclusive Global Growth.” The summit will culminate with the release of the New Delhi Declaration.2:35 pm: Closed-door session for BRICS member countries on “Inclusive Global Governance and Strengthening Multilateralism”.4:25 pm: Leaders will tour the Bharat Innovates Exhibition.5:05 pm: Leaders will assemble at Bharat Mandapam for the family photo, followed by a joint tree-planting ceremony.7:30 pm: Prime Minister Narendra Modi will host a gala dinner for the leaders.9:55 am: Leaders from BRICS member countries, partner nations and outreach invitees will begin arriving.10:35 am: Official group photo.10:50 am: Open session on “Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability: Shaping the Future for Inclusive Global Growth”.The summit will conclude with the release of the New Delhi Declaration.Chinese President Xi Jinping, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Russian President Vladimir Putin, South African President Cyril Ramaphosa and Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto are among the leaders expected to attend the summit, reported PTI.The summit comes against the backdrop of the global economy facing disruptions from the Russia-Ukraine war, the West Asia crisis, including concerns over the Strait of Hormuz, and the trade and tariff policies of the Trump administration.With the grouping operating on consensus, questions also remain over whether members will agree on a joint statement, particularly amid differences between Iran and the UAE over the West Asia crisis.BRICS originally comprised Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa. The group expanded in 2024 to include Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia, while Indonesia joined in 2025.Belarus, Bolivia, Kazakhstan, Cuba, Malaysia, Nigeria, Thailand, Uganda, Uzbekistan and Vietnam became BRICS partner countries in 2025.The grouping now has 11 member countries, representing around 49.5% of the world's population, 40% of global GDP and 26% of global trade, according to the Indian government.India assumed its fourth BRICS chairship on January 1 this year having previously chaired the grouping in 2012, 2016 and 2021.India's chairship is guided by the theme “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability”, with a stated focus on a people-centric approach rooted in the principle of “humanity first”.Under India's chairship, more than 350 meetings and high-level engagements have been held across more than 25 cities, covering the grouping's three broad pillars: political and security cooperation, economic and financial cooperation, and cultural and people-to-people exchanges.
Article Summary: Two-day brics summit in new delhi will focus on food and energy security, health, disaster resilience and critical supply chains. Summit, hosted by india under its 2026 chairship, will also cover trade, investment, connectivity and technology. Leaders will exchange views on global and regional developments.

Article Title: Creating a multi-layered security grid in Delhi, one Brics at a time
Article Text:
Creating a multi-layered security grid in Delhi, one Brics at a time

NEW DELHI: When the 'Flying Kremlin' and other ultra-secure aircraft touch down in Delhi this weekend, they won't just bring Russian President Vladimir Putin and other high-profile world leaders to the Brics Summit, they will land with a fully autonomous fortress-on-wheels featuring personal food-testing labs, decoy dignitaries and armoured limousines built to survive landmines and chemical attacks.As Delhi transforms into an impenetrable, multi-layered defensive grid, security personnel are bracing for a high-stakes security operation where AI-aimed snipers scan rooftops, gesture-recognition cameras spot human posture shifts, commandos slither down ropes from hovering helicopters and anti-graffiti strike teams patrol the streets 24/7, guarding against everything from high-tech threats to stealth protest tactics.The capital, sources said, hasn't seen security this tight since the 2023 G20 summit, and preparations this time are even more extensive. Unmanned aerial vehicles have been categorised as one of the most potent threats, and systems that can jam drone signals or shoot them down have been installed at several locations.Every dignitary or their hotel or carcade has been assigned a code name or call sign to ensure they are guided smoothly between locations without any overlap or security glitches.Intelligence inputs have hinted at the possibility of flash protests and spray-painting of inflammatory slogans near the venues, targeting some foreign leaders. Cops have formed anti-graffiti teams for round-the-clock patrolling to thwart any such attempts.President Putin's security grid comprises a sophisticated protective shield managed jointly by Russia's Federal Protective Service (FSO) and Indian counter-terrorism forces. Ground mobility will be centred around his custom-made, heavily armoured Aurus Senat limousine, often referred to as a "rolling bunker". Transported directly from Moscow, the state car is built to withstand chemical attacks, landmines and sniper fire, complete with run-flat tyres and an independent emergency oxygen supply.Up in the air, the Russian leader travels in a specially modified Ilyushin IL-96-300PU aircraft, known as the "Flying Kremlin", which operates alongside decoy jets, advanced missile-defence countermeasures and secure command systems. On the ground, the innermost protective layer comprises elite officers from Russian Presidential Security Service (SBP), supported by advanced FSO teams that sanitise every scheduled and potential itinerary venue. The Russian delegation manages its own strict logistics, travelling with personal chefs, portable testing laboratories for food and drink, and measures to collect biological waste, alongside deploying dummy dignitaries in select hotels to boost operational security.Securing the designated summit hotels in central Delhi, Aerocity and Gurgaon presented one of the most formidable logistical challenges for intelligence and law enforcement agencies. Every hotel is being managed as an independent secure zone under its assigned DCP venue commander, supervised by special commissioner-rank officers overseeing broader zones.Within each hotel, two rooms have been repurposed into operational command posts: a primary security control room linked directly to Delhi Police's central C4i command node and a secondary contingency room dedicated to emergency management.To prevent unauthorised access, advanced AI cameras equipped with posture-detection and intrusion-alert software monitor perimeter walls and hallways, capable of flagging unusual physical movements like crawling or wall-scaling. Hotel staff have undergone rigorous multi-round background checks conducted by special branch and special cell, with movement restricted strictly to assigned floors using specially programmed digital keycards.
Article Summary: The capital hasn't seen security this tight since the 2023 g20 summit. Ai-aimed snipers scan rooftops, gesture-recognition cameras spot human posture shifts. Unmanned aerial vehicles have been categorised as one of the most potent threats.

Article Title: Brics to kick off with talks to boost multilateralism
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: PM Narendra Modi will host a gala dinner for the leaders participating in the Brics summit on Saturday evening, said govt in an announcement Wednesday. The summit will formally begin earlier in the day with Modi welcoming the leaders of Brics member states at the venue, Bharat Mandapam, and later joining them for a closed session titled Inclusive Global Governance and Strengthening Multilateralism.India is hosting the 18th Brics summit on Sept 12-13, exactly 20 years after the grouping that counts 11 major emerging economies as members was formalised. After the session, the leaders will witness the Bharat Innovates exhibition at the summit venue, before congregating on the outside lawns for a Brics family photo. This event will be followed by leaders participating in a joint tree plantation.Modi is also expected to have a formal bilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping Saturday in which both leaders will look to consolidate gains from the recent uptick in bilateral ties. Xi had last visited India in 2019 for the Mammalapuram informal summit. A formal announcement by Beijing about Xi's visit was still awaited on Wednesday.Modi's bilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin is scheduled for Friday. The PM is also expected to have a meeting with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian. UAE will likely be represented by Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan.Bridging bilateral divides over the West Asia situation to secure a unified Brics declaration remains the primary hurdle for India, ahead of the meetings.On Sunday - second day of summit - Modi will welcome leaders of the 10 Brics partner countries, along with other outreach invitees. The leaders will join the final session titled Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability: Shaping the Future for Inclusive Global Growth.The summit will see a renewed call by Modi for a reinvigorated, inclusive and effective multilateral order at a time when the world is faced with complex challenges. As EAM S Jaishankar had said, Brics needs to commit to a reformed multilateralism that reflects contemporary realities - one where institutions like United Nations, WTO, IMF and World Bank are representative and inclusive.
Article Summary: India is hosting the 18th brics summit on sept 12-13, exactly 20 years after the grouping that counts 11 major emerging economies as members was formalised. The summit will formally begin earlier in the day with modi welcoming the leaders of brics member states at the venue, bharat mandapam.

Article Title: India considers it a responsibility, not a favour, to provide aid to Sri Lanka as first responder: Rajnath to president Dissanayake
Article Text:
Defence minister Rajnath Singh meets Sri Lankan president Anura Kumara Dissanayake

Defence minister Rajnath conveyed greetings on behalf of PM Modi and underlined that the citizens of the two countries share deep friendship based on strong historical and civilisational links and people-to-people exchanges. He emphasised that as a closest friend and neighbour of Sri Lanka, “India considered it not a favour, but a responsibility to provide assistance as the first responder and would continue to do so in the future as well”.Sri Lankan president Dissanayake said his country would never allow its territory to be used for activities inimical to India’s security interests. He also expressed his gratitude for the relief assistance provided by India as part of Op Sagar Bandhu during Cyclone Ditwah and the comprehensive rehabilitation package extended by New.Both leaders virtually inaugurated three Bailey bridges constructed by the Indian defence forces. The two sides also exchanged MoUs on upgradation of L70 guns for the Sri Lankan Air Force, and cooperation between NCC and National Defence Colleges of both the countries.Rajnath also met Sri Lankan PM Harini Amarasuriya. “We exchanged views on a range of issues related to development cooperation, education and close cultural and civilisational ties,” he posted on X.He underlined that as “sister democracies with shared heritage”, India and Sri Lanka should continue working towards a shared developmental vision for the peace and prosperity of the region. Rajnath also highlighted Sri Lanka's importance in India's Vision MAHASAGAR, saying the island nation holds a special place in the policy and would continue to do so in the future.Rajnath called for enhanced cooperation between India and Sri Lanka to shape a favourable and secure maritime environment and tackle emerging maritime challenges before they evolve into serious threats to developmental interests and brighter future. “Secure sea lanes, freedom of navigation, respect for international law and unhindered maritime trade are pivotal for collective security & prosperity of the Indian Ocean Region (IOR),” the defence minister said while addressing a gathering comprising Sri Lankan deputy minister of defence Aruna Jayasekara, commanders of the Sri Lankan three services.Rajnath said India and Sri Lanka are bound by the shared ocean, and maritime security is not a matter of abstract theory but a reality that shapes their trade, security and destinies. “Both nations are central to any strategic discourse on maritime security in the region. Strong India-Sri Lanka maritime cooperation will be mutually beneficial and vital for collective growth and security,” he said.Referring to the challenges faced by our fishermen, the defence minister underscored that the issue needs to be addressed together. He observed that maritime cooperation should extend beyond the security framework to also cover areas like aquaculture, marine biotechnology, ocean science, protection and preservation of maritime environment and maritime tourism.He also suggested that the two countries can explore the establishment of a joint Maritime Humanitarian Assistance & Disaster Relief (HADR) system involving relevant agencies for a coordinated and rapid response to natural calamities and man-made disasters.Rajnath also laid a wreath at the Indian Peace Keeping Force (IPKF) Memorial in Battaramulla and paid homage to the bravehearts who made the supreme sacrifice in the line of duty.
Article Summary: Defence minister rajnath singh meets sri lankan president anura kumara dissanayake. Both leaders virtually inaugurated three bailey bridges constructed by the indian defence forces. The two sides also exchanged mous on upgradation of l70 guns for the sri lanka air force and cooperation between ncc and national defence colleges.

Article Title: ‘Making memes’: P Chidambaram says Gen Z is having last laugh over PM Modi’s ‘naraaz fufa’ jibe
Article Text:

‘Naraaz Fufa’ jibe over freight corridor

NEW DELHI: Former Union minister and Congress leader P Chidambaram on Wednesday hit back at Prime Minister Narendra Modi over his recent remarks targeting the Opposition, saying he was “happy” and “proud” to be called a “Dimagi Naxal” and describing the “Naraaz Fufa” remark as meaningless.Speaking to news agency ANI, Chidambaram said, “I'm happy that I'm not a Bewakoof Naxal. I'm happy that I am a Dimagi Naxal.”Calling PM Modi a “self-confessed poet”, Chidambaram said the Prime Minister often coins slogans and expressions and later translates them into English.“He is a self-confessed poet. He writes poetry in Gujarati. I think he coins these words in Gujarati and translates them into English. I read the translation into English, but this is his way,” Chidambaram said.“He started by saying, ‘acche din aane wale hain’. Then I counted the slogans he had coined. I think there are something like 20-25 slogans in the last 12 years. The latest two are the ‘Dimagi Naxal’ and ‘Naraaz Fufa’,” he added.Chidambaram said PM Modi's remarks had generated discussion on social media, particularly among Gen Z users.“Tomorrow, he will say something. At the Brics Summit, he will say something. But these are meaningless.I am told that Gen Z has made a lot of memes on ‘Naraaz Fufa’ and ‘Dimagi Naxal’. When I tweeted that I'm proud to be a Dimagi Naxal, the likes were 5.5 million,” he said.“I don't know whether all of them claim to be Dimagi Naxals, but at least a substantial number of them liked the tweet, which means they are also Dimagi Naxals,” he added.Chidambaram had earlier reacted to PM Modi's “Dimagi Naxal” remarks in a post on X, writing, “I am proud to be a dimagi naxal!”Chidambaram's comments came after PM Modi, in his Independence Day address from the Red Fort, urged people and authorities to “identify and isolate” those with a “dimagi naxal” or ideological Naxal mindset.The Prime Minister said government action since 2014 had largely ended jungle insurgency, which had claimed the lives of more than 3,500 security personnel. He also alleged that people with a “Maoist mentality” had earlier held positions in government committees and influenced policy.PM Modi said armed Maoist violence was “breathing its last”, but an ideological Naxal mindset continued to exist in some institutions. He also warned against allowing such a mindset to influence the country's youth.The Congress leader's remarks also came a day after PM Modi revived his “Naraaz Fufa” jibe at critics of government initiatives while addressing a ‘NaMo for Viksit Bharat’ event in Vadodara.Highlighting the benefits of double-stack container freight trains, PM Modi said a recent service from JNPT in Mumbai to Vadodara carried cargo equivalent to more than 250 trucks.“Recently, a double-stack container freight train was operated from JNPT (Mumbai) to Vadodara—meaning the train ran with one container stacked on top of another. With this single trip, the volume of cargo transported from Mumbai to Vadodara was equivalent to that of over 250 trucks. Now, enter the 'naraaz fufa' figure—the one who will immediately start complaining: ‘What about the truck drivers? Where will the trucks go? What will happen to those who bought trucks?’ Well, 'fufa' has found something to grumble about now,” he said.PM Modi also said the Dedicated Freight Corridor would reduce travel time and logistics costs while saving fuel and benefiting the environment. He said work on the 2,800-kilometre corridor had been completed and that the Eastern and Western Dedicated Freight Corridors were becoming the “backbone” of India's trade and commerce.PM Modi has previously used the “Naraaz Fufa” expression while addressing the centenary celebrations of Delhi University's Shri Ram College of Commerce.At the event, he described critics of government initiatives as people who questioned the need for new projects. Referring to the world's tallest statue, high-speed trains and UPI, the PM said the same “Phoofas” had repeatedly asked what the need for such initiatives was.Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge had also criticised the Prime Minister's remarks at SRCC, saying he was giving the opposition “a new adjective every” year.Kharge listed terms including “Naraz Fufa, Dimaagi Naxal, Urban Naxal, Khan Market Gang, Andolan-jiwi” and “Parjivi”, and accused the government of using such labels while avoiding questions from the youth.The exchange over “Dimagi Naxal” and “Naraaz Fufa” has since added two more expressions to the ongoing political sparring between the BJP and Congress.

Article Title: Mahmood Farooqui on Storytelling, Survival and the Human Cost of Imprisonment
Article Text:
Q: Let's start with the art of storytelling.

A:

Q: When you were in Tihar prison, you put together a motley crowd of amateur actors, many of them illiterate, and you had nothing, and yet you brought this about. Let's talk about that.

A:

Q: How does the language of the performance shift?

A:

Mahmood Farooqui is an acclaimed writer and performer known for reviving Dastangoi, the lost art of Urdu storytelling. He has received the Ramnath Goenka Award for Besieged: Voices From Delhi-1857. He has been visiting fellow at the University of Michigan and University of California, Berkeley. Mahmood has co-directed Peepli Live and produced The Great Shamsuddin Family. In this conversation, he discusses 'The Tihar Players'. Excerpts from the interview:When I began work on reviving this or studying about it, I had never seen anyone perform Dastangoi because the last Dastango passed away in 1928. I was very blessed to have the scholarship and the guidance of the great Shamsur Rahman Faruqi, one of the greatest writers, novelists, critics and poets that modern Urdu, or indeed modern India, has produced. But he had also never seen somebody perform. So when we tried to put up the first show, we had the stories, but we had nothing to emulate or no model. So it was really our intuition... that put together the first modern show...And of course, the stories themselves were phenomenal. You know, the story, the fantasies of tricksters and sorcerers, nothing of that kind of imagination and fertility and fecundity has been written anywhere in the world, as far as I know... And then, of course, I started writing my own stories, I started doing workshops. So today, 21 years later, we have. Now the word 'dastan' is back in the currency of our usage in a huge way...We live in a multicultural society. We live in a multilingual society. So any text that I approach, whether I'm working on the Mahabharata or the Ramayana,... many writers in different languages, many literatures have worked on those things. So whenever we present the Mahabharata, people are startled that there are so many versions of the Gita in Urdu or the Mahabharata in Urdu or in Persian, there are so many poems to odes to Lord Krishna, similarly for Ramayana. It's all our legacy. The world of Sanskrit, the world of Persian, the world of Urdu, the world of medieval Hindi. And we bring all that together in the spoken word...I had to do something which in prison terms in India is called mashakkat — rigorous imprisonment. So I went to the education ward and I proposed that I should set up a theatre class... You might think, what is the point of this? You know, my case is more important. I'm very tortured, as everybody in prison is. You know, everybody is suffering. Everybody has got a plethora of problems because there are court cases to deal with, there are families to deal with. There are problems inside prison. There is food, there is medical health. So amongst all those problems and preoccupations, if somebody's saying, come and do theatre with me, it seems a little odd...And then people started getting into it with workshops. When I started, you know, getting them to play out scenes from their own life, from their prison life, then they started enjoying the catharsis... I would consider myself immensely blessed and fortunate that I could see them grow as actors grow in confidence. And it did wonders to their own self esteem. Many of them have benefited from it. Now they're outside, they're working, whether as instructors, public speakers or you know, photographers. And also it did wonders to the atmosphere inside prison because a prison is a very coercive space... We were fighting not so much to be artists, but to restore our own humanity and to find dignity which came to us on stage, which came to us as performers when we saw the gleam in people's eyes, when we saw that for moments when we were doing the Ram Leela, people forgot about everything that was troubling them and they were lost in it.I took a Premchand Munshi called 'Nasha' which we improvised completely. It was a device play. So we brought in a lot of prison lingo...When we did 'Charandas Chor', I tried to retain as much as possible the Chhattisgarhi dialect there because when that dialect was understood by people in Edinburgh, why wouldn't people in Delhi understand it? When I did Molière, I lampoon prison doctors inside... I coined a song about paracetamol. You're dying, you get paracetamol...All the capital and social and cultural capital that I had accumulated outside was of zilch value inside... Nothing really mattered because we had all been reduced to the bare bones of being a human being where we were all being shoved and abused, not just by authoritarian orders or officers, but also inmates. Because always, everywhere, there is a chain of violence that comes from top down, and then you replicate it, then you bully others in turn. When you are stripped of everything that you know, everything that makes your identity, how do you form your identity and where do you stand? How do you say that you know who you are? And I was lucky that my drama class began to believe in me. They began to respect me. They formed a core around me, and I was able to find a place in prison without money, without clout, which is not a mean gift, you know...And when I lived there, I realised people may have committed acts which are illegal, which are maybe reprehensible... Every day they know their families are suffering... There is disgrace, there is suffering, there is deprivation. Sometimes their children have to leave school, sometimes they have to change addresses. Their families sometimes travel hours and upon hours to just come and meet them. So a person's conduct outside does not mean that a person has ceased to be a human being. And second, we send people to prison as punishment. So once a person is inside prison, the person has been punished because a person has been confined. A person has been deprived of their family, of food, of comfort, of a phone, of hugging their children, of hugging their dog, sitting on their chair, having a morning chai. So many everyday things and textures they've already been deprived of when they are inside prison.The law and rules and regulations also follow them inside prison. So people are sent to prison as punishment. But within prison also, they are being punished. Their mulakat might be taken away. Where they are staying might be shifted. Their court cases are inflicting suffering on them. So there is an infinite everyday addition of suffering and punishment and retribution that a person inside is already going through. Regardless of what is happening with their trial, they are suffering humiliation, they are suffering loss of respect, they are suffering insults, they are suffering loss of food, loss of romance, loss of women, loss of hope, loss of time, loss of opportunity. So when you are inside, you're already suffering regardless of the outcome of the case.
Article Summary: Mahmood farooqui is an acclaimed writer and performer known for reviving dastangoi. He has received the ramnath goenka award for besieged: voices from delhi-1857. Mahmood has co-directed peepli live and produced the great shamsuddin family. All the capital and social and cultural capital that i had accumulated outside was of zilch value inside.

Article Title: ‘Civilisational twins’: Rajnath Singh meets Sri Lankan president, steps up India’s defence ties with Colombo

NEW DELHI: Defence minister Rajnath Singh on Wednesday met Sri Lankan President Anura Kumara Dissanayake in Colombo and discussed the multi-faceted partnership between the two countries, including cooperation to ensure the safety, security, peace and prosperity of the region.Singh arrived in Sri Lanka on Tuesday for a three-day visit. His visit is the first by an Indian defence minister to the island nation in 38 years.Singh conveyed Prime Minister Narendra Modi's greetings to Dissanayake and congratulated him on the completion of two years of his government. He also underlined the deep friendship between the people of India and Sri Lanka, based on their historical and civilisational links.“The two sides reaffirmed that as civilisational twins, close neighbours and maritime partners, India and Sri Lanka would continue to work together for their development and welfare of the people while working jointly to ensure the safety, security, peace and prosperity of the region,” the ministry of defence said.Singh described the meeting as “warm and extremely productive” in a post on X.Dissanayake recalled his interactions with Prime Minister Modi and reiterated that Sri Lanka would never allow its territory to be used for activities inimical to India's security interests, the ministry of defence said.The Sri Lankan president also expressed gratitude for India's relief assistance under Operation Sagar Bandhu during Cyclone Ditwah and the comprehensive rehabilitation package extended by New Delhi for reconstruction and rehabilitation.Singh said India considered assistance to Sri Lanka a responsibility rather than a favour.“As a closest friend and neighbour of Sri Lanka, India considered it not a favour, but a responsibility to assist as the first responder and would continue to do so in the future as well,” he said.Both leaders also virtually inaugurated three Bailey Bridges constructed by Indian defence forces.India and Sri Lanka exchanged memorandums of understanding on the upgradation of L70 guns for the Sri Lankan Air Force and cooperation between the National Cadet Corps (NCC) and National Defence Colleges (NDC) of both countries.The MoU on the upgradation of six L70 guns for the Sri Lankan Air Force falls under an Indian government grant. The Ministry of Defence said the upgraded air defence guns would strengthen the air defence architecture of critical assets in Sri Lanka.The guns had earlier been provided to the Sri Lanka Air Force by India.The academic cooperation agreement between the NDCs of India and Sri Lanka will facilitate knowledge sharing between the two institutions, the ministry said.The NCC cooperation agreement will formalise the NCC youth exchange programme between India and Sri Lanka. The programme provides an opportunity for NCC cadets from multiple countries to travel to New Delhi each year and participate in NCC events.Singh is leading a high-level delegation comprising senior officials from the ministries of defence and external affairs.Singh's visit also included an interaction with the Indian diaspora in Colombo, where he said India would stand firmly with Sri Lanka during times of crisis.“The relationship between India and Sri Lanka is based on shared history, culture, and faith. We stand with Sri Lanka through thick and thin and are committed to the peace, prosperity, and development of both countries,” Singh said, according to news agency ANI.Sri Lanka's leader of opposition Sajith Premadasa also praised India's support for the island nation after meeting Singh, describing India as a “very close partner” and the bilateral relationship as “very special”.“My meeting with Rajnath Singh was very constructive, very progressive. We have a very strong relationship with India. It is a special relationship. We are very close partners,” Premadasa said.He highlighted India's role as a first responder during Sri Lanka's economic crisis, the Covid-19 pandemic and Cyclone Ditwah.“India has always been the first responder. And Prime Minister Modi has always walked the talk. India has been the first responder in supporting Sri Lanka during Ditwah, during times of bankruptcy, and during the Corona health hazard,” Premadasa said.Premadasa said Colombo wanted to further deepen ties with India while respecting the sovereignty, territorial integrity and political independence of both countries.

Article Title: Strategic Autonomy in motion as India hosts 18th BRICS Summit
Article Text:
This would be the 18th summit of the grouping. (Photo: ANI)

India for BRICS

Key Challenges for India

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

India will host the annual BRICS summit on September 12-13 at Bharat Mandapam, returning to the venue where it held the G20 summit in 2023. That gathering is remembered for the inclusion of the African Union in G20, marking a major step in efforts to bridge the gap between the Western-led global order and the emerging Global South. At BRICS, India will look to leverage that momentum, working with major emerging economies to demand structural reforms of global governance institutions dominated by the West.This would be the 18th summit of the grouping that brings together 11 major emerging and developing economies – Brazil, Russia, India, China, South Africa, Ethiopia, UAE, Indonesia, Iran, Egypt and Saudi Arabia – along with 10 other partner countries. Together, BRICS nations account for 49 percent of world population, 40 percent of global GDP and 26 percent of international trade.The last time India hosted an in-person BRICS summit was in 2016 in Goa. This year also marks 2 decades of formalisation of the bloc for cooperation on issues related to global economic and political governance. The theme of India's 2026 chairship is Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability, drawing inspiration from PM Narendra Modi's 'humanity first' and people-centric approach to BRICS.This will also be the first summit to see in-person participation by Russian President Vladimir Putin since the start of the Ukraine war. Chinese President Xi Jinping is also visiting India for the first time in 7 years to participate in the summit.Under its chairship, India has so far held over 350 meetings - 25 at the ministerial level including the foreign ministers and national security advisers’ engagements. The ministerial meetings have so far resulted in key outcomes and initiatives spanning agriculture, health, energy, environment, disaster management and also trade, reaffirming commitment to a fair, inclusive and transparent multilateral trading system with WTO at its core.Despite the political fragmentation and economic imbalances associated with the grouping, BRICS remains important for India for multiple reasons, especially in an increasingly uncertain world. For one, it lends India a platform to practice its strategic autonomy and multi-alignment policy, not allowing any one single bloc to acquire excessive leverage over it. That it can simultaneously expand its strategic and technology ties with the West and also work with Quad for a free and open Indo-Pacific reinforces an independent foreign policy. For India, as external affairs minister S Jaishankar has said, BRICS is an embodiment of a multipolar world. India is not giving up on its Western partnerships, only hedging against uncertainty whether from US unpredictability or Chinese ascendancy.BRICS also allows India to showcase its Global South leadership credentials, as it works with other major emerging markets to push for reforms of global institutions like the UNSC, IMF and World Bank that are not representative of the developing world. Support for UNSC reforms is important, although it still falls short of an explicit endorsement of India's permanent membership bid, mainly because of China's presence.India's approach to BRICS is also guided by its complex ties with China. Turning away would mean allowing China to single-handedly shape the agenda of the developing world. BRICS is consensus driven and even for Washington and other Western capitals, India's moderating influence should be of significance as it prevents the bloc from turning into an anti-West platform.There's focus as well on expanding financial architecture as no government would like its trade to be held hostage by instruments it can't control. As Jaishankar has underlined, institutions such as the New Development Bank and the Contingent Reserve Arrangement demonstrate the group's ability to create credible alternatives. For India, these are not initiatives targeted at any currency. In any case, India has officially said it's against de-dollarisation or any attempt to target the US currency. It has also ruled out any proposal for a common BRICS currency.BRICS provides India with markets, along with trade diversification, de-risking and supply-chain opportunities. According to a commerce ministry press release, intra-BRICS merchandise trade reached approximately $1.17 trillion in 2024. India exported an estimated $82 billion in goods to BRICS members in FY2025–26, alongside approximately $31.3 billion in services exports in 2024. BRICS membership deepens India’s trade relationships with Russia (energy), Brazil (agriculture/commodities), Gulf and African countries, diversifying away from overreliance on any single partner.The first of course is to forge a consensus on West Asia that would enable a joint BRICS declaration, a task complicated by the presence of the UAE and Iran in the group. India would not like the event to end with a Chair's Statement, like what happened with the foreign ministers' meeting, knowing well that no BRICS summit has concluded without a comprehensive joint declaration. Foreign secretary Vikram Misri said last week India has received cooperation from all members and the government is working to arrive eventually at a constructive outcome that benefits all BRICS stakeholders. India will focus on drafting a resolution rooted in the UN Charter, dialogue and diplomacy, freedom of navigation and civilian protection, while looking to ringfence economic agreements from contentious political issues by acknowledging respective national positions.Balancing relations with the US is another key concern for India, which is hosting the summit fresh off a tariff firestorm with Washington. US President Donald Trump sees the grouping itself as an assault on the US currency and has threatened to impose 100 percent tariffs on BRICS nations if they work to replace the US dollar. India backs legitimate local-currency settlement, while maintaining it is against any common BRICS currency or China-centered replacement mechanism. As it walks the diplomatic tightrope, India must steer initiatives like the integration of central bank digital currencies (CBDCs) but without appearing to endorse any anti-dollar bloc.Another challenge for India is to prevent China's predominance without destabilising its bilateral relations with Beijing. For all the talk about BRICS' combined power, China enjoys a vastly asymmetrical influence with its trade, investment, manufacturing and critical mineral leverage. Wary of China's efforts to advance its own economic interests, India has not endorsed SCO’s 2030 economic roadmap and it must find a way to work with China in BRICS on shared objectives but without allowing the forum to be co-opted as a Chinese economic or geopolitical platform.This also intersects with the challenge of ensuring that an expanded grouping remains governable and cohesive, especially with countries like Pakistan and Bangladesh pursuing membership with support from Beijing. True multipolarity and consensus-driven equality within the organisation are key imperatives for India.As Jaishankar said while announcing India's summit agenda, BRICS must transition now from a forum for discussions to a platform for delivery. In that spirit, India seems focused on delivering an outcome-oriented summit with key deliverables like a unanimous BRICS declaration, logistics supply-chain cooperation framework, incubator/ startup network, development finance, cross-border payment and continued support for Indian priorities like UNSC reforms and counterterrorism.To conclude, inclusion of the African Union was not the only major takeaway from the G20 summit in 2023. Perhaps more dramatic was the last-minute consensus on Ukraine through a compromise language crafted by India, allowing a G20 declaration. India can take confidence from that diplomatic triumph, heading into another tough but potentially rewarding global summit.
Article Summary: India will host the annual brics summit on september 12-13 at bharat mandapam. The theme of india's 2026 chairship is building for resilience, innovation, cooperation and sustainability. This would be the 18th summit of the grouping that brings together 11 major emerging and developing economies.

Article Title: US President Donald Trump drops vehement criticism on Dallas Mavericks’ Luka Doncic trade: “It might go down as the worst trade in the history of sports”
Article Text:

Donald Trump delivers harsh verdict on Luka Doncic trade 19 months later

How Luka Doncic's trade changed the Mavericks and the NBA

The Luka Doncic trade is not winding down, as it has found a new critic. The president of the United States, Donald Trump , stopped by the Dallas Mavericks' home arena Wednesday night and told a packed room he still can't make sense of the deal that sent Doncic west.Trump was speaking at American Airlines Center during the Republican National Committee's midterm convention, and basketball wasn't even the point of the night. He brought it up anyway and went on to compare Dallas trading away its franchise star to one of the most infamous sales in baseball history.Nineteen months after the trade went through, Donald Trump stood inside the building where Doncic used to play and admitted the whole thing still baffles him. His remarks came on the opening night of the RNC's two-day midterm convention, the first time the event has been held at the Mavericks' arena. Lee Greenwood's "God Bless the USA" was still fading out as Trump walked onstage around 8:10 p.m.He was upfront about not being a basketball expert. That didn't stop him from delivering a verdict anyway. Trump said, "This is a big Dallas Mavericks team, which is going to be hopefully good.I must tell you, I don't understand the trade. That trade is not, what do I know about basketball? I would say it's not going to go down as the greatest trade in the history of sports. It might go down as the worst trade in the history of sports. "Further, the President went on to compare the Red Sox-New York Yankees wild 1919 Babe Ruth trade, "Babe will always be the worst trade. But is it Luka? Maybe we could redo that trade. I redo deals all the time. We gotta redo that deal. I don't get that deal. Some deals you understand; I understand deals. But that one I didn't quite get."The trade closed on February 2, 2025, and it was bigger than a straight one-for-one swap. It was actually a three-team deal that also pulled in the Utah Jazz. Dallas sent Doncic to Los Angeles and got back Anthony Davis, Max Christie, and a 2029 first-round pick. Nine months later, the Mavericks fired general manager Nico Harrison, the man who built the trade, and handed the front office to Michael Finley and Matt Riccardi.Three months after the trade, Dallas won draft lottery luck and took Cooper Flagg first overall. Flagg started every game he played as a rookie, averaging 21.0 points, 6.7 rebounds and 4.5 assists, and won Rookie of the Year. Davis lasted only 20 games in Dallas before a February 2026 trade sent him to Washington, while Christie stuck around and shot 40.4 percent from three across 77 games. The Mavericks are still in the puzzle and attempting to rebuild the roster.The Mavericks still finished 26-56. Masai Ujiri took over basketball operations in May, hired Mike Schmitz away from Portland, and parted ways with coach Jason Kidd soon after. Dusty May now runs the bench. Doncic, meanwhile, is averaging 31.9 points, 7.8 rebounds, and 8.1 assists across 92 games in Los Angeles, numbers that make Trump's frustration easy to understand, even if the front office saw it differently.Following the trade, there were huge protests by fans, and certainly, it was one of the most talked-about trades in history, as it has also garnered attention from Trump.
Article Summary: Donald trump delivers harsh verdict on luka doncic trade. Trump: "i don't understand the trade. That trade is not, what do i know about basketball? I would say it's not going to go down as the greatest trade in the history of sports"

Serena Williams sold her long-held Bel-Air estate for $8.1 million in April 2019, ending a sale process that lasted about 18 months. The tennis star had bought the property in 2006 for $6.612 million and first listed it in late 2017 for $11.995 million, or nearly $12 million. The 1935-built home sits on about 2.7 acres and has 6,101 square feet of living space, six bedrooms and seven bathrooms. Williams later reduced the asking price to $9.995 million, but the property eventually changed hands for $8.1 million, giving her a gross gain over what she originally paid.Serena Williams bought the Bel-Air property in 2006 for $6.612 million, according to property records reported by The Washington Post. At the time, the home gave her a large private space in one of Los Angeles’ most well-known luxury neighborhoods.The house was built in 1935, so it was not a newly constructed celebrity mansion when Williams bought it. Instead, the property had an older California feel, with plenty of land around the main house. Its location in the Stone Canyon area also gave the estate a level of privacy that is difficult to find on a large residential property in Los Angeles.Williams kept the home for more than a decade. During those years, her life changed in major ways, both on and off the tennis court, while the Bel-Air house remained one of her main Los Angeles properties.Williams put the property on the market in late 2017 with an asking price of $11.995 million. The timing came after she welcomed her daughter, Olympia, in September 2017, and married Alexis Ohanian.Around the same period, Williams and Ohanian bought a newer home in the Beverly Hills area for about $6.7 million. That five-bedroom property was built with features aimed at modern family living, including a pool, wine cellar and yoga room.The move meant Williams no longer needed to keep the older Bel-Air estate as her main Los Angeles home. The Bel-Air house was much larger in terms of land, but the newer property offered a different kind of setup for the family.The initial $11.995 million price was also well above what Williams had paid for the house. At that figure, the estate was being offered for roughly $5.4 million more than its 2006 purchase price.The Bel-Air home had six bedrooms, seven bathrooms and about 6,101 square feet of living space. It was built across a large, tree-filled property, giving the house a more private setting than its street address might suggest.Inside, the home had marble and hardwood floors, high ceilings and a large living room. The living room included a curved wall of clerestory windows and French doors that opened toward the greenery outside. There was also a dark wood executive office or study and a wet bar.The main bedroom area was larger than a standard bedroom suite. It included a sitting area, dressing rooms and a large bathroom.One of the home’s more unusual features was a full-service hair salon. That stood out even among the property’s other luxury features and suited Williams’ busy life in tennis, fashion and public appearances.The estate also had a gym and a three-car garage. Outside, the grounds included a swimming pool, pool house, gardens, covered patio areas and private walking trails.Despite being owned by one of tennis’ greatest players, the property didhave a tennis court.The original $11.995 million asking price did not bring a sale quickly. After the property had spent months on the market, Williams cut the price by about $2 million in April 2018.The new asking price was $9.995 million. That was still nearly $3.4 million above the $6.612 million Williams had paid for the home in 2006, but it was a major step down from the original listing.The house continued to sit on the market. By the time it sold, the final price was much lower than both of the earlier asking prices.The Los Angeles Times reported that the property finally sold for $8.1 million in April 2019. That meant Williams accepted about $3.895 million less than the original $11.995 million asking price.On the basic purchase price alone, Williams still made money from the sale. She paid $6.612 million for the property in 2006 and sold it for $8.1 million in 2019.That puts the difference at about $1.488 million before expenses linked to the sale, such as commissions, taxes and other closing costs. So the $8.1 million transaction was not a loss compared with her original purchase price.At the same time, the final sale was far below the number Serena Williams had hoped to get when she first listed the home. The gap between the initial asking price and the final sale price was close to $3.9 million.For a property that stayed with Williams for about 13 years, the final deal therefore tells two different parts of the story: she did not get close to the original $12 million target, but she also sold the estate for more than she had paid for it.The Bel-Air sale closed a long chapter in Williams’ Los Angeles real estate history. The 2.7-acre property had been part of her life since 2006, but after her family grew and her housing plans changed, the older estate was eventually sold for $8.1 million.
Article Summary: Serena williams bought a 2.7-acre bel-air estate with a 6,101-sq-ft mansion in 2006 for $6.612 million. The tennis star put the property on the market in late 2017 with an asking price of $11.995 million. After repeated price cuts, it sold for $8.1 million after being listed for nearly $12 million.
